articles.full_text:
Arman Gukasyan is the founder and chief executive of Revizto
Every heatwave in the UK brings the same headlines: power plants shutting down, rail speed restrictions, schools sent home early, hospital equipment overheating. With 2026 the hottest year on record in the UK, none of this is a surprise or bad luck. It’s the predictable result of infrastructure that was built for a climate that no longer exists.
The industry’s usual response has been to patch rather than rebuild. That approach was defensible when extreme heat was rare, but it isn’t anymore. The costs of patching are stacking up faster than anyone budgeted for in lost productivity, damaged materials, and stalled sites.
The UK currently has a £148bn infrastructure funding gap to close by 2040. Every pound spent on new or upgraded infrastructure is a chance to build for the climate we actually have, but only if resilience is designed in from the start.
And even when resilience and sustainability are top priorities, projects can unravel over time. Coordination issues at the design stage can prevent the best plans from becoming reality.
The good news is that many of these failures are preventable: a clash between a duct run and a structural beam, a specification that doesn’t account for thermal expansion, or a services layout that assumes a cooling capacity the building won’t have.
The cost of catching them in a model – in time, money and disruption – is a fraction of what it costs when the system fails mid-heatwave. That’s the real argument for digital adaptation: not efficiency for its own sake, but the fact that the cheapest moment to fix a coordination failure is on a screen, before anyone breaks ground and not in a control room above 35°C when the cooling system trips.
Where the real cost sits
In extreme heat, the physical toll on site teams is real and evident: asphalt, steel and heavy machinery all amplify already extreme temperatures, and when conditions cross the safety threshold, sites shut down entirely. But the quieter damage is logistical. Materials don’t perform reliably in extreme heat, margins are already thin, and the industry is dealing with supply chain bottlenecks and skills shortages leaving little room for further delays.
At the heart of this is a simpler problem: fragmentation. Asset blueprints and records often still sit on paper or may not exist at all. By the time the heatwave hits, it’s not easy to make quick fixes. That’s why a single, shared digital source of project data matters more than it used to. Centralising information is what enables teams to catch rework before it happens, and make repairs to existing assets more efficiently.
Loading…
A new lens on technology
Construction technology is usually discussed in terms of return on investment, productivity and margin protection. Those still matter. But extreme weather is now forcing a different framing: digitalisation as a means for resilience, not just efficiency.
Controlling the pace of climate change is a huge challenge. But we can control how well we understand our vital infrastructure – and how quickly we can act when the next extreme weather event hits.
With billions needed for new and upgraded infrastructure over the next decade, technology that enables centralised data and unified workflows could be the difference between building for the climate we used to have and the one we’re living in now.

Every heat-preparedness calendar that American communities, utilities, and hospitals built around "summer" is now running about six weeks behind the actual danger window. A landmark climate study published in late September 2026 in Nature Climate Change documents that the global heatwave season — the span from a year's first heatwave to its last — has expanded by roughly 39 days across the world's land surface since 1979, with danger arriving weeks earlier in the spring and lingering weeks deeper into fall than it did for the previous generation.
The expansion matters in two ways that compound each other. First, it is widening the calendar window during which heat-stressed systems — agricultural fields, electrical grids, hospital emergency departments, human bodies — must remain on alert. Second, the study identifies a more recent and troubling trend in that same expanded window: the first heatwave of any given year, the one that arrives before acclimatization and before city cooling centers have reopened for the season, is increasingly peaking on day one. The time available to warn people is shrinking at the exact moment the danger period is growing.
The structural implication is concrete: a household, a municipality, or an emergency manager operating on a traditional June-through-August heat-risk frame is now systematically under-protected at both ends of the year.
Season Bookends: How the Study Measured Change
The research, led by Wenfang Xu of the South China Botanical Garden at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, drew on ERA5 — a global climate reanalysis dataset produced by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) that reconstructs hourly atmospheric conditions worldwide at roughly 31 kilometers (19 miles) of horizontal resolution. The dataset spans 1979 to 2023, giving the team 45 years of near-complete planetary temperature coverage. A reanalysis dataset differs from a simple weather record: it combines observed measurements from satellites, ground sensors, and weather balloons with physics-based atmospheric modeling to produce a globally consistent retrospective — meaning no data gaps over oceans or sparsely instrumented regions. ERA5's consistency over the full study period is what makes trend analysis of this scope possible.
The team's definition of a heatwave was precise and locally calibrated: three or more consecutive days in which the daytime high temperature fell in the top 10% for that specific calendar date at that specific location. That relative, date-specific threshold is the methodological key to the entire analysis. Rather than asking "was it above 95 degrees Fahrenheit (35°C)?" the study asked "was it hotter than 90% of all the days this date has ever recorded here?" A 75°F (24°C) day in Montana in March could qualify. A 105°F (41°C) day in Phoenix in August might not, if August is when Phoenix routinely reaches 105°F (41°C). The approach specifically captures heat that is dangerous because it is out of season, not merely because it is hot in absolute terms. The relative threshold methodology is central to why the study's findings are globally consistent.
The team then identified the first and last heatwave of each hemisphere's warm season — May through September in the Northern Hemisphere, November through March in the Southern — and tracked how those bookends shifted over 45 years.
The results were consistent across the globe. The first heatwave of each year moved about 3.3 days earlier per decade. The final heatwave pushed about 5.4 days later per decade. Combined, those two trends add nearly nine days of heatwave season every ten years. Across the 45-year study period, that compounds to the headline figure: 39 additional days of heatwave-season exposure compared to 1979. Approximately 92% of global land area trended toward longer heatwave seasons, with roughly a third of land showing a statistically significant lengthening.
Two independent temperature datasets — including data from Berkeley Earth, a nonprofit climate science organization that produces its own global temperature reconstructions independent of government agencies — confirmed the same pattern, significantly strengthening the finding's credibility.
Why Do Arid Zones Change Fastest?
Not all landscapes are shifting at the same pace. The study found that arid zones — deserts and dry grasslands — are outpacing humid regions by a substantial margin.
In the driest areas, the first heatwave of the season now arrives roughly 6 days earlier per decade, approximately 2.4 times the pace observed in humid zones. At the other end of the season, the final heatwave in very arid places is ending more than 8 days later per decade — about one and a half times the global average rate. The arid-zone acceleration figures suggest moisture-related feedback mechanisms are driving the divergence.
A likely mechanism, which the study identifies as a candidate explanation without formally quantifying it, is soil moisture feedback. Dry soils have less water available to evaporate, which means less of the sun's energy goes toward cooling and more goes toward raising air temperature. As arid zones dry out earlier in the spring, they heat faster — which may explain why the first heatwave arrives sooner and why arid regions are accelerating at both ends simultaneously.
The geographic picture becomes granular at the regional level. Northern and central Europe, the Caribbean, and southern Central America saw the season's final heatwave shift more than 10 days later per decade. Eastern Europe, the Mediterranean, northwestern North America, and northern Africa are gaining heat exposure at both ends of the season simultaneously. In South Asia, the dominant shift has been at the tail end of the season; in western North America and South Africa, it has mostly been at the front.
What Is a Rapid-Onset Heatwave — and Why Is the Share Growing?
Beyond the season's expanding duration, the study identified a more recent trend: a growing share of the year's first heatwave that peaks on the very first day.
Researchers classified each year's initial heatwave by how quickly it developed to its maximum intensity. A rapid-onset event hits its peak temperature immediately, on day one. A slow-building one ramps toward its maximum over several days, giving the affected population more time to adapt. Over the full 45-year study period, the mix of fast, medium, and slow first heatwaves remained roughly stable. But since 2001, the proportion of rapid-onset first heatwaves has been increasing by about half a percentage point per decade.
The trend is modest in size but outsized in consequence. A heatwave that peaks on day one gives emergency managers, hospitals, and individuals almost no lead time to respond — and it specifically disadvantages the population groups most dependent on warning time: older adults, outdoor workers, people without air conditioning, and those with cardiovascular or respiratory conditions. Rapid-onset events also tend to arrive earlier in the season, compounding the exposure by hitting when no one is physiologically acclimated to high temperatures yet.
Research on this phenomenon predates the Xu study. A 2010 Yale mortality study of 43 US cities found that the first heatwave of a season raised the daily risk of non-accidental death by approximately 5%, compared to roughly 2.65% for later-season heatwaves of similar intensity — a nearly doubled mortality premium for early, unacclimatized heat exposure.
Xu put the implication directly in her own words: "In the past, we have mostly focused on whether heatwaves are becoming more frequent, stronger, and longer. Our study further shows that their timing and onset speed are changing. If heatwaves arrive earlier and develop more rapidly, the time available for societies and ecosystems to prepare and adapt could become even shorter."
These trends also converge with what real 2026 data are already showing. UK public health surveillance reported approximately 2,877 heat-associated excess deaths in May and June 2026 — nearly double the total for all of 2025. An early May event contributed an estimated 753 deaths, while an extended eight-day June event contributed another 2,124, with both months exceeding all previous temperature records and triggering national red alerts before many seasonal heat-preparedness measures were active.
Farms and Grids Are Already Absorbing the Costs
The study examined where the expanded heatwave calendar is translating into measurable economic damage.
Agriculture faced a complex picture. Farmland was the one land-use category where earlier heatwave arrival was not statistically significant — but the calendar shift is still showing up in crop vulnerability. The share of global cropland exposed to heatwaves during critical reproductive phases — flowering, pollination, grain fill — grew by between 1.6 and 13.3 percentage points when comparing 2001–2023 against the 1979–2000 baseline. Heat exposure during early growth and near-harvest stages increased as well, extending the portion of the crop calendar that requires heat-risk management. These figures are from the study's crop analysis of major global staple crops.
The researchers cited Europe's 2018 growing season as a case study in what happens when these timing shifts collide with critical phenological windows. Heat and drought struck during the flowering period of wheat and barley across the continent, and nearly 40% of cultivated European land produced yields in the bottom tenth of its historical record that year.
Energy infrastructure is also facing structural pressure from the extended season. A 2025 heatwave across southern Europe drove air-conditioning demand up by as much as 14% in some areas, while average power prices nearly doubled — a concentrated illustration of what longer heat seasons will demand of electrical grids that were built for a narrower peak-demand window.
What Did the Study Decline to Measure?
The authors are specific about the study's limitations, and two are editorially important.
First, the study tracked daytime high temperatures only, excluding the warm nights that doctors and emergency physicians increasingly identify as the more dangerous component of extended heat events. Overnight heat prevents the body from recovering between hot days — a physiologically critical process for older adults and people with cardiovascular disease. A 2026 Nature Climate Change study by Rebecca Emerton and colleagues at ECMWF, using a Universal Thermal Climate Index that incorporates humidity, wind, and radiation alongside temperature, found that the warmest nights are warming faster at a rate of 0.32°C (0.58°F) per decade, faster than the warmest ten days at 0.27°C (0.49°F) per decade. The Xu study's 39-day figure is likely a conservative lower bound on the full human health burden of the expanding danger window.
Second, the study measured when heatwaves happened and did not attempt to quantify why the season is shifting. The team identifies greenhouse-gas-driven background warming, the persistence of blocking high-pressure systems that lock heat in place, and earlier-season soil drying as plausible interacting contributors — but the study did not parse each driver's relative contribution. That attribution question remains open for future work.
How Much Time Is Left to Fix Warning Systems?
The study closes with what may be its most direct policy finding: the expanding season demands that heat-alert systems be redesigned around the new calendar, not the old one.
The United Nations' "Early Warnings for All" initiative, co-led by the World Meteorological Organization, aims to protect every person with an early warning system by the end of 2027 — a deadline now 15 months away. As of November 2025, 119 countries, or 60% of all nations, had reported multi-hazard early warning systems, according to the WMO and UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction's most recent Global Status Report. But only 26 countries have climate-informed heat-health early warning systems specifically, and roughly one-third of the world's population still lacks coverage under any multi-hazard warning system — a figure the WMO has characterized as "unacceptable." The 2023 State of Climate Services Health report documented both the 26-country figure and the coverage gap in detail.
The Xu study's two parallel findings make the 2027 deadline harder to meet: more of the year now falls within the danger window, expanding the period these systems must operate, and early-season events are increasingly the type that peak too fast for conventional warning lead times to catch. A warning system calibrated to flag hot days in July does nothing for a rapid-onset April heatwave in Spain or a September event in the Pacific Northwest — both of which, under the season-timing trends documented here, fall squarely within the expanding danger band.
The study does not prescribe a specific policy response. What it establishes is the evidence base: warning systems that track only peak-summer temperatures, food-security models built on historical growing-season heat norms, and grid-demand forecasts anchored to a June-August danger window are all working from a map that no longer matches the territory.
What Does This Mean for Rapid-Onset Events Specifically?
Among all the study's findings, the rapid-onset trend carries the most direct implication for public health infrastructure. Standard heat-alert protocols depend on a sequence that takes time: forecasters identify developing heat, meteorological agencies issue alerts, health departments activate cooling centers and outreach to vulnerable populations, and individuals take protective action. That chain requires at least 24 to 72 hours of lead time to function effectively — time that a heatwave peaking on day one does not provide.
The Xu study does not quantify how much of this lead-time gap has already been eroded, and the dataset ends in 2023 — before the 2026 heatwave season that has already set new early-season mortality records in the UK. What the study does establish is the direction of travel: the events with the least warning time are becoming a larger share of the first, most dangerous heatwaves of each year.
A related 2026 study by Catherine Ivanovich of NASA's Goddard Institute for Space Studies, published in AGU Advances, found independently that extreme heat has spread into spring and fall across more than half of the world's land area since the 1980s, with the pattern varying by region: the US Southwest and southeastern states have seen heat extend later into fall, while the Gulf Coast has seen it arrive earlier in spring. Taken together, the two studies — using different methodologies and different timeframes — converge on the same finding: the danger calendar of extreme heat has fundamentally shifted, and preparedness systems have not caught up.
Frequently Asked Questions
Why does it matter that the heatwave season is starting earlier and ending later, rather than just getting hotter?
Because the whole infrastructure of heat protection — cooling centers, hospital surge planning, agricultural heat insurance, grid demand forecasting, public health outreach to vulnerable populations — is designed around a "summer" window that no longer matches when the danger arrives and departs. Early-season heatwaves are more deadly per unit of intensity than mid-summer ones: research on 43 US cities found the first heatwave of a summer kills at roughly twice the rate of later-season events of the same temperature and duration, because people haven't acclimated and protective systems aren't yet active. Six extra weeks of danger window means six extra weeks of exposure to that elevated early-season risk — and the study documents that this expanded window is a global trend, not a regional anomaly.
What is a rapid-onset heatwave, and why is the share of them rising?
A rapid-onset heatwave is one that hits its peak temperature on the very first day, rather than building over several days toward a maximum. The Xu study classified each year's first heatwave by how quickly it develops, and found that since 2001 the proportion that are rapid-onset has been steadily increasing. The likely contributors involve soil moisture dynamics: drier soils — which are themselves a product of earlier-season heat drying ground that would historically still be moist — absorb solar energy faster because there is less water to evaporate, driving air temperatures up more quickly. The consequence for preparedness is that the heat events arriving earliest in the season, when people are least ready, are also the events that allow the least time between "this is developing" and "this has already peaked."
Does this affect the US specifically?
Yes, and with regional variation. The study found that northwestern North America and eastern parts of the US are gaining heat exposure at the front end of the season — meaning earlier spring heatwaves — while other areas are seeing extension into fall. A related 2026 study from NASA's Goddard Institute found that the US Southwest and Southeast have seen extreme heat days extending later into the fall specifically, while Gulf Coast states are experiencing earlier spring heat, with humid-heat events (which impair the body's ability to sweat-cool) arriving before the summer months. Neither of these regional patterns is well-served by warning systems and preparedness programs calibrated to a traditional June-August frame.
How close is the world to meeting the UN goal of universal heat warning coverage by 2027?
Further than the calendar suggests. As of November 2025, 60% of countries had some form of multi-hazard early warning system, but only 26 countries had climate-informed heat-health systems specifically. Roughly one-third of the global population remains without any multi-hazard warning coverage — a group that is disproportionately concentrated in least-developed countries and small island states, the same regions where heat risk is climbing fastest. The UN "Early Warnings for All" initiative has 15 months remaining on its 2027 deadline. The Xu study's finding that the danger window is simultaneously expanding and front-loading with faster-developing events makes the technical challenge of meeting that deadline more demanding than it would have been even five years ago.

Early-season heatwaves are more deadly per unit of intensity than mid-summer ones: research on 43 US cities found the first heatwave of a summer kills at roughly twice the rate of later-season events of the same temperature and duration, because people haven't acclimated and protective systems aren't yet active. Six extra weeks of danger window means six extra weeks of exposure to that elevated early-season risk — and the study documents that this expanded window is a global trend, not a regional anomaly.
What is a rapid-onset heatwave, and why is the share of them rising?
A rapid-onset heatwave is one that hits its peak temperature on the very first day, rather than building over several days toward a maximum. The Xu study classified each year's first heatwave by how quickly it develops, and found that since 2001 the proportion that are rapid-onset has been steadily increasing. The likely contributors involve soil moisture dynamics: drier soils — which are themselves a product of earlier-season heat drying ground that would historically still be moist — absorb solar energy faster because there is less water to evaporate, driving air temperatures up more quickly. The consequence for preparedness is that the heat events arriving earliest in the season, when people are least ready, are also the events that allow the least time between "this is developing" and "this has already peaked."
Does this affect the US specifically?
Yes, and with regional variation. The study found that northwestern North America and eastern parts of the US are gaining heat exposure at the front end of the season — meaning earlier spring heatwaves — while other areas are seeing extension into fall. A related 2026 study from NASA's Goddard Institute found that the US Southwest and Southeast have seen extreme heat days extending later into the fall specifically, while Gulf Coast states are experiencing earlier spring heat, with humid-heat events (which impair the body's ability to sweat-cool) arriving before the summer months. Neither of these regional patterns is well-served by warning systems and preparedness programs calibrated to a traditional June-August frame.
How close is the world to meeting the UN goal of universal heat warning coverage by 2027?
Further than the calendar suggests. As of November 2025, 60% of countries had some form of multi-hazard early warning system, but only 26 countries had climate-informed heat-health systems specifically. Roughly one-third of the global population remains without any multi-hazard warning coverage — a group that is disproportionately concentrated in least-developed countries and small island states, the same regions where heat risk is climbing fastest. The UN "Early Warnings for All" initiative has 15 months remaining on its 2027 deadline. The Xu study's finding that the danger window is simultaneously expanding and front-loading with faster-developing events makes the technical challenge of meeting that deadline more demanding than it would have been even five years ago.
